docs.title: Health Without Borders — Frontend
docs.text: Flutter cross-platform client for the Health Without Borders initiative.

docs.title: What is this project?
docs.text: Health Without Borders is a mobile and web application designed for vulnerable populations (migrants, rural communities) operating in environments with limited connectivity. The frontend captures medical records in the field using NFC device, stores them locally in SQLite, and automatically synchronizes them with the backend when a connection is available.

docs.title: Design Principles
docs.text:
• Offline-first: The synchronization engine runs in the background when a network connection is detected.
  • NFC como identificador: Each patient is linked to an NFC device (unique UID). Read/write operations use nfc_manager.
  • Contrato de API estricto: The domain models in lib/src/features/nfc/domain/patient_record.dart are a 1:1 mirror of the backend schemas (FastAPI).
  • Roles y permisos: Access to functionalities is controlled by UserRole (doctor, nurse, org_admin, superadmin).

docs.title: Unit tests (test/unit/)
docs.text:
These tests test pure business logic, without UI. They use repository mocks when necessary.

Recommended pattern:

void main() {
  group('AuthRepository', () {
    late AuthRepository repo;
    late MockApiClient mockClient;

    setUp(() {
      mockClient = MockApiClient();
      repo = AuthRepository(apiClient: mockClient);
    });

    test('login stores token on success', () async {
      when(mockClient.postForm(...)).thenAnswer(
        (_) async => {'access_token': 'fake-token'},
      );
      final session = await repo.login(email: 'a@b.com', password: 'pass');
      expect(session.email, 'a@b.com');
    });
  });
}

docs.title: API and Domain
docs.text:
This section documents the domain models, the HTTP client, and the authentication flow.

  • Domain Models — Dart classes that mirror the backend schema.
  • HTTP Client — ApiClient, error handling, timeouts.
  • Authorization — login, JWT token, roles, and permissions.

docs.title: HTTP Client — ApiClient
docs.text:
lib/src/core/network/api_client.dart

ApiClient is the centralized network layer. All repositories use it; no one calls http.Client directly.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
final apiClient = ApiClient(baseUrl: AppEnv.apiBaseUrl);

baseUrl is read from the environment variable API_BASE_URL defined in .env.

docs.title: App version header
docs.text:
Every request carries X-App-Version with the build, for example 1.2.3+45 (android) (lib/src/core/network/app_version.dart). The backend logs it on login and refresh, so the team can see which build each device runs before an NFC key rotation (security review N5).

Flutter does not expose --build-name/--build-number to Dart, so the build passes the version as a define. The release pipeline (release.yml) does it for every platform; a manual build must add it too, or it sends no header and the backend logs app_version=none:

flutter build apk --release --build-name=1.2.3 --build-number=45 \
  --dart-define=HWB_APP_VERSION=1.2.3+45 --dart-define=ENV_FILE=.env.production

The platform suffix (android, ios, web) is added by the app. A value outside MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH[+BUILD] sends no header.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
When the server responds with a code >= 300, ApiClient throws ApiException:

class ApiException implements Exception {
  final String message;
  final int? statusCode;
}

The detail property of the backend JSON response is used as the error message when available.

Example of handling in a repository:

try {
  final data = await apiClient.postJson(...);
  return PatientSyncResponse.fromJson(data);
} on ApiException catch (e) {
  if (e.statusCode == 401) {
    // Expired token — redirect to login
  }
  rethrow;
}

docs.title: Timeout
docs.text:
All requests have a 20-second timeout by default. After this time, http.Client throws a TimeoutException that repositories must catch.

POST /api/v1/patients/sync uses 90 seconds (PatientRepository.syncTimeout): the server codes diagnoses with the LLM and writes to the FHIR Store inside the request (p95 25.6 s, up to 68 s in production). A timeout does not mean the record was not saved; the sync engine retries, which is safe, and the retry may come back with stale_payload_base_version.

docs.title: HTTP Client Injection (testing)
docs.text:
ApiClient accepts an optional http.Client. This allows a mock to be injected into tests:

final mockClient = MockClient((request) async {
  return http.Response('{"access_token": "fake"}', 200);
});

final apiClient = ApiClient(baseUrl: 'http://test', client: mockClient);

docs.title: Login Flow
docs.text:
LoginScreen
    │
    ▼
AuthRepository.login(email, password)
    │
    ├── POST /api/v1/login/access-token  (form-encoded)
    │       → { access_token: "..." }
    │
    └── GET /api/v1/users/me
            → UserSession { id, email, fullName, role, organizationId }

The JWT token is persisted in FlutterSecureStorage with the key hwb_access_token. On app restart, AuthRepository.getCurrentUser() attempts to retrieve the token and rebuild the session.

docs.title: UserSession
docs.text:
class UserSession {
  final String id;
  final String email;
  final String fullName;
  final UserRole role;
  final String organizationId;
  final String? organizationName;
  final bool isActive;
  final bool mustChangePassword; // set by an administrator: change it first

  String get shortName; // First two words of fullName
}

docs.title: Password change
docs.text:
AuthRepository.changePassword(currentPassword, newPassword) calls POST /api/v1/users/me/password. The server ends every session of the user, this device's included, and answers with a new token pair and NFC keyring (the same shape as the login response); the repository stores them in place of the old ones. A refresh that was already in flight with the revoked token does not end the session.

  • 400: the current password is wrong. The screen refuses a new password equal to the current one before sending, so that is the only 400 left.
  • 422: the new password breaks the policy. PasswordPolicy checks it in the app first: at least 12 characters, at most 72 bytes in UTF-8, not a common password.
  • 429: too many attempts, by IP or login_paused with Retry-After (5 wrong passwords in 15 minutes pause the account; the pause also blocks the login).

must_change_password comes in the login, refresh and GET /users/me responses. It is true for accounts an administrator created and after a reset. While it is true, Home and every route open ChangePasswordScreen(mandatory: true): no way back, only change the password or sign out.

The backend agrees: on a temporary password it answers only GET /users/me, the password change, refresh and logout; every other route gets 403 with code password_change_required. So SyncEngine sends nothing while mustChangePassword is set (a 403 would block the queued records for good), and a password_change_required from /sync stops the batch and leaves every row as it was, like user_inactive. The session that comes back from the change starts the engine again.

Administrators reset a password with UserRepository.resetPassword(id) (POST /api/v1/users/{id}/reset-password): superadmin, or org_admin for the doctors and nurses of their organization. The temporary password is shown once.

A login refused with 429 (login_paused or the per-IP limit) tells the user how long to wait (ApiErrorCode.tooManyAttempts).

If the backend does not return full_name, the repository constructs it by humanizing the email: "doctor.juan@org.com" → "Doctor Juan".

docs.title: Token Security
docs.text:
• The token is stored exclusively in FlutterSecureStorage — on iOS it uses the Keychain, on Android the Android Keystore.
  • It is Never stored in SharedPreferences or the flat file system.
  • The SyncEngine stops the entire synchronization process upon receiving a 401 error and delegates the re-login to the UI.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
This section describes how the code is organized, what each layer does, and how data flows from NFC capture to synchronization with the backend.

  • Project Structure — directory tree and conventions.
  • Modules and Features — description of each feature in lib/src/features/.
  • Offline-First and Synchronization — local data flow → backend.
  • NFC Encryption and Key Ring — wire format, key ring, session window and build compatibility.

docs.title: ADR 001: Decision on TLS Certificate Pinning
Status
docs.text: Approved

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The Health Without Borders mobile application communicates with the backend API over HTTPS. An audit finding (fe-oct26-sin-pinning-tls) highlighted that the ApiClient currently relies on standard system trust stores rather than implementing strict TLS Certificate Pinning.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
We decided to rely on standard system CA trust stores combined with active client-side transport security controls, while deferring strict Certificate Pinning unless required by enterprise MDM / policy mandates.

The app enforces transport security using the following active mechanisms: 1. Enforced HTTPS in Release Mode: ApiClient and AppEnv reject any http:// API base URL during release builds, failing closed immediately. 2. Disabled Redirect Following: ApiClient executes HTTP requests with followRedirects = false. Any 3xx response triggers an ApiException regarding untrusted redirects, avoiding portal interception. 3. Captive Portal Probing: Reachability.probe validates that connection responses yield expected 2xx status codes and JSON headers before attempting sync operations.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Pros:
  • Avoids app bricking during backend SSL certificate rotations or domain migrations in offline/intermittent field environments.
  • Allows field devices managed by enterprise MDM solutions to use private internal CAs when necessary.
  • Cons / Risks:
  • High-privilege attackers with compromise over a device's root CA store could theoretically intercept traffic.
  • Mitigation:
  • Sensitive PHI stored on chips and offline database remains independently encrypted with AES-256-GCM.

docs.title: ADR 002: Decision on Web Offline Capability and Architecture Scope
Status
docs.text: Approved — amended 2026-10-16 (see "Amendment")

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Audit finding fe-oct26-web-no-funciona-offline noted that the Flutter Web build uses default service worker behavior (unregistering self) and fetches CanvasKit resources from Google CDN (www.gstatic.com). Consequently, the Web application shell cannot bootstrap without an initial network connection.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: We decided to define Flutter Web strictly as an Online Administrative Console, while reserving full Offline-First Field Capabilities exclusively for the native Android and iOS mobile applications.

docs.title: Key Guidelines
docs.text:
1. Web Scope: The Web target is intended for organization administrators (superadmin, org_admin) and web-connected clinical staff conducting online searches, analytics reviews, and user/organization management.
  2. Mobile Scope: Native mobile applications (Android/iOS) remain the sole offline-first targets equipped with SQLite local storage, encrypted offline queues, and background synchronization drivers.
  3. Service Worker & CDN: We retain standard online bootstrap mechanics for Web builds rather than bundling self-hosted CanvasKit assets and offline service worker caching in the Web bundle.

docs.title: Amendment (2026-10-16): what the Web build still stores locally
docs.text:
The original text said Web eliminates local browser PHI persistence. The code does not support that claim: LocalDatabase keeps a Web branch backed by IndexedDB (hwb_local_store, via web_storage_js.dart), the sync engine starts on every platform, and web_storage_js.dart documents that it persists the offline queue and the emergency audit trail on Web.

What is true, and is now the documented behaviour: - The application shell is online-only (guideline 3 is unchanged): without a first connection the Web app does not start. - Once running, a Web session that loses connectivity can still queue edits in IndexedDB. Those records are encrypted with AES-256-GCM before they are stored, and are removed when they sync. - On Web the AES key that protects that queue lives in the browser (flutter_secure_storage on Web keeps it in sessionStorage per tab; session lifecycle is tied to the browser tab). Encryption at rest on Web therefore protects against casual inspection of IndexedDB, not against script running in the same origin. - Shared workstations: logout must wipe the queue and the key. This is a release criterion for the Web build, not an assumption.

docs.title: Consequences (replaces the original "Pros")
docs.text:
• Simpler deployment, CSP and asset distribution (unchanged).
  • Prevents stale web application shells from executing outdated offline logic (unchanged).
  • Web does not remove PHI persistence in the browser; it limits it to an encrypted, short-lived queue. If that is not acceptable for shared terminals, the alternative is to remove the Web branch of LocalDatabase and make Web saves online-only (a code change, to be decided separately).

docs.title: ADR 003: Binding NFC Payloads to the Chip
Status
docs.text: Proposed

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Audit finding fe-oct26-payload-nfc-no-ligado-al-chip: the AES-256-GCM payload is authenticated only with its version header (and with an empty AAD for version 0). It does not include the chip UID, the record type or the time it was written, and chips stay writable. A payload copied to another chip still decrypts, and an old payload put back over a newer one hides what was added since.

Constraint from docs/architecture/nfc-encryption.md: every chip in the field is version 0, headerless, and no rotation has happened. Builds that predate versioning read version 0 with an empty AAD, so version 0 cannot change until the whole fleet understands a new format. A version 1+ payload is unreadable by older builds already, so no chip of that kind exists in the field.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Version 1+ payloads are sealed with the chip UID and the record MIME type as extra AAD (chipBindingAad in nfc_payload_service.dart). On read, the service tries that AAD first and then a plain decode, which is what keeps version 0 chips readable. A v1+ payload moved to another chip, or relabelled with another MIME type, fails authentication on both attempts.
  2. Version 0 stays unbound. The residual risk (cloning a v0 chip to another chip) remains until the deployment rotates to version 1, following the existing fleet rule: keep the current key version at 0 until every device runs a build that understands the ring and the binding. With the backend's ring in its database (KEK mode, as on the pilot) that means not calling /patients/nfc-keys/rotate and leaving NFC_AUTO_ROTATE off; NFC_CURRENT_KEY_VERSION applies only without a KEK.
  3. Writing a bound payload needs the UID. When expectedUid is given the payload is encoded before the tap (the tap is refused on any other chip). Otherwise it is encoded inside the tap, with the chip's real UID.

docs.title: Not decided here (needs product / backend input)
docs.text:
• writtenAt in the payload. A timestamp alone cannot reveal a replay offline: it only helps when compared with a trusted value (the last version the device synced). Define that comparison before adding the field.
  • NTAG21x password protection against malicious erasure. It requires a platform-level write sequence that the current nfc_manager wrapper does not expose and has to be validated on real chips.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Pros: from the first rotation, cloned or relabelled payloads are rejected; version 0 chips keep working; builds can be mixed during the rollout because nothing written today changes.
  • Cons: until rotation, the protection does not apply to the chips already in the field. A chip written with binding is read by one more decrypt attempt on failure (negligible). When rotation happens, tests with real chips are required.

docs.title: Acceptance
docs.text:
• test/unit/nfc_chip_binding_test.dart passes: a v1+ payload does not decrypt with another UID, another MIME type or no AAD; a v0 payload still reads without AAD.
  • Before any rotation, run the checklist in the backend NFC key-management runbook and confirm the fleet.

docs.title: ADR 004: NFC Chip Model for Patient Devices
Status
docs.text: Proposed — covers the temporary test batch only; the official chip model and quantity are still to be evaluated

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Audit finding fe-oct26-triaje-no-cabe-en-ntag213. The triage NDEF message measures 193 B with no allergies and 332 B with 6 allergies and 4 chronic conditions. Usable NDEF capacity by chip:

Chip Usable NDEF capacity Fits the triage message NTAG213 about 137 B No (not even the empty triage) NTAG215 about 492 B Yes NTAG216 about 872 B Yes

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Patient devices require NTAG215 or NTAG216. NTAG213 is not supported.

  • Model purchased: NTAG215 (K LAKEY, 50 pcs, black round PVC tags, 25 mm, 504 B total memory) — supplier / order reference: none; label code X0032K29BT. Temporary test batch only: 22 units in use for field and lab testing, the rest kept as spare.
  • Existing NTAG213 stock: none. No NTAG213 tag is in use or in stock; if any is found, it is withdrawn and not issued.
  • date: 2026-10-19 — approval covers the test batch only. The official chip model and quantity are still to be evaluated before the project goes live.

docs.title: What the app already does
docs.text:
• nfc_triage_payload.dart documents the NTAG215/216 requirement.
  • NfcPayloadService measures the whole NDEF message against the capacity the chip reports and throws NfcPayloadTooLargeException with the sizes; on a chip of 180 B or less the message says that an NTAG213 was detected and that NTAG215/216 must be used.
  • Guardian cards are fitted to the chip's real capacity (buildWithinCapacity), keeping the most recent consultations and vaccines and leaving none out while there is room for it (see "How the guardian copy is fitted to the chip" in nfc-encryption.md); the triage payload is not trimmed, by design.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A tap with an NTAG213 fails with a clear message instead of a write error halfway.
  • Any future triage field has to be checked against the 492 B of NTAG215, the smaller of the two supported chips.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Proposed. Phase 1 (every build reads format 2, writes format 1) is implemented; phase 2 (writing format 2) needs the fleet check below and its own change.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The NFC compression audit measured the current pipeline (JSON map → CBOR → DEFLATE → AES-256-GCM in a MIME record) on 600 synthetic records built with the app's own builders. DEFLATE itself is close to the best general-purpose compressor at these sizes: zstd, brotli and LZMA2 do not beat it by more than 7 %. What makes the payload large is the method around it:

  • No preset dictionary. Payloads of 100 to 2,000 bytes give DEFLATE no history to draw on: the triage compresses from 122 B to 120 B. Most of what a payload holds (keys, codes, frequent values) repeats from one patient to the next, which is what a dictionary shared by writer and reader supplies.
  • Values stored as text. UUIDs of visits and vaccines are 10 % of a compressed guardian copy and dates 4 %: as text they are close to incompressible.
  • A long record type. application/vnd.hwb.triage and application/vnd.hwb.guardian cost 29 to 34 bytes per chip.

The guardian copy is where this hurts. Median message sizes: 496 B with no history, 1,112 B with one consultation and one vaccine. On an NTAG215 (492 B) not even the base fits in 54 % of the records, and an NTAG216 (872 B) holds a consultation in practically none (ADR 004, ADR 006).

dart:io adds a trap: ZLibEncoder(raw: true, dictionary: d) ignores the dictionary and produces the same bytes as without it. A round-trip test still passes, because the decoder ignores it too.

docs.title: Record
docs.text:
One NFC Forum external record (TNF 0x04) per chip:

Payload Format 1 (MIME) Format 2 (external) Patient device application/vnd.hwb.triage guane.com.co:hwbt Guardian device application/vnd.hwb.guardian guane.com.co:hwbg

The record type is also what tells a reader which format it has, and it is the type string the chip binding of ADR 003 puts in the associated data. The record overhead drops from 29–34 B to 20–23 B. The domain is Guane's; another owned domain can replace it before phase 2, never after.

docs.title: Payload
docs.text:
The encryption is exactly that of format 1 (NfcPayloadCodec.seal/open): key ring, version header from version 1, chip binding, nonce and tag. Only the plaintext changes:

[format = 2][dictionary id][raw DEFLATE stream primed with the dictionary]
  1. Map. The same map format 1 writes: the triage of NfcTriagePayload, the aliased guardian copy of NfcGuardianPayload.buildWithinCapacity. Builders, fitting and reconstruction do not change.
  2. Typed CBOR. For a fixed set of keys per kind of payload (nfc_payload_v2.dart, _typing), a value in exactly the canonical shape is stored as what it is. Anything else stays text, so nothing is lost:
Shape Stored as Triage keys Guardian-copy keys lower-case UUID 16-byte string — pid, ei, vid chip UID as read (04:A1:…) byte string gUid, g2Uid dug YYYY-MM-DD days since 1900-01-01 dob dob, dte YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS±HH:MM [seconds since 2020-01-01, offset / 15 min] — sd, ed, aat digits, no leading zero, ≤ 18 integer docN, gPh dn, ph, rc, nit, cyc, nc
  1. DEFLATE with a preset dictionary, level 9, raw: the stream zlib produces after deflateSetDictionary, readable by any zlib with inflateSetDictionary (checked against Python's zlib). Since dart:io will not prime a raw stream, the writer compresses the dictionary, flushes to a byte boundary (Z_SYNC_FLUSH) and keeps only what follows; the reader inflates its own compressed form of the dictionary first. The stream depends only on the dictionary's content, not on how either side compressed it (a test reads it after priming at another level).

Nothing is written that does not read back. NfcPayloadV2.encode decodes its own output and compares it with the input, strictly on types; when they differ it throws and the write fails with NfcWriteException. Every payload of the audit corpus (3,000, triage and guardian copies with 0 to 3 consultations and vaccines) reads back exactly.

docs.title: Dictionaries
docs.text:
nfc_payload_v2_dictionaries.dart holds them: 8,165 B for the triage and 30,704 B for the guardian copy, the size where each stops gaining (the guardian copy gains up to the 32 KB DEFLATE window, the triage barely past 8 KB). tool/nfc_payload_v2/build_dictionaries_test.dart builds them, reproducibly, from the typed CBOR of 400 synthetic training records of the audit corpus.

  • No patient data, ever. The repository and the app are public, and a dictionary built from real records would ship fragments of them in every install. A dictionary is built from synthetic records, public catalogs (ICD-10, vaccines, DIVIPOLA, EPS) and text written for the purpose.
  • A dictionary is part of the format. Once a build has written with dictionary n, every later build reads it. A better dictionary gets a new id; the bytes of an id never change. Tests pin each one by SHA-256.
  • Dictionary 1 is a candidate until phase 2. The audit measured it on synthetic text. Before it is frozen, measure real note lengths with tool/nfc_measure (audit recommendation 3) and decide whether to rebuild it.

docs.title: Rollout
docs.text:
Chip written by Read by builds before this ADR Read by builds with it Format 1 ✅ ✅ Format 2 ❌ (seen as a blank chip) ✅
  1. Phase 1, this change. Every build reads both formats and writes format 1. --dart-define=HWB_NFC_PAYLOAD_FORMAT=2 makes a build write format 2, for field tests with chips that only those test devices read.
  2. Fleet check. The backend logs X-App-Version on login and refresh: wait until every device in use runs a build with phase 1. The write-size telemetry (nfc_write_metrics, payload format 1) shows which chips are written and how full they get.
  3. Phase 2, its own change. Switch the default of kNfcWriteFormat to format 2. Chips change format as they are rewritten.

Going back to writing format 1 is always possible; dropping the reading of format 2 is not, while any chip may hold it. The same rule as key rotation (nfc-encryption.md, "Updating the fleet") applies, for the same reason: a build that cannot read a chip treats it as blank.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Phase 1 changes nothing on the chips: builds can be mixed.
  • A build before phase 1 that meets a format 2 chip sees it as blank. That is why phase 2 waits for the fleet check.
  • The app carries 38 KB of dictionaries (58 KB of source).
  • Each write and each fit estimate compresses the dictionary first: about 0.2 ms per estimate on a laptop, a few ms on a phone, inside the tap.

docs.title: Acceptance
docs.text:

  • test/unit/nfc_payload_service_test.dart, group "formato 2": external record written and read, a format 1 build reads it, a format 2 build reads format 1, the budget of the external record, chip binding with key version 1, devices of another patient refused, a damaged record read as blank.

docs.title: ADR 006: What the Guardian Copy Carries
Status
docs.text: Proposed — needs a product decision on each group below

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The guardian device holds a bounded copy of one patient's record (NfcGuardianPayload.buildGuardianPayload): the shape of PatientFullRecord.toJson() without the consent signature and without the AI metadata of diagnoses, with at most the three most recent consultations and the three most recent vaccines. Offline, the app opens that copy editable when it belongs to the patient device just scanned (read_nfc_screen.dart), and what is edited there syncs later through the backend merge (app/services/record_merger.py in the backend repository).

Guardian devices are NTAG215 (492 B of NDEF) or NTAG216 (872 B) (ADR 004). The NFC compression audit measured the copy on a synthetic corpus built with the app's own builders (200 test records, the app's DEFLATE, the app's capacity budgets of 458 B and 838 B):

  • without any history the copy needs 496 B (median, whole NDEF message), so on an NTAG215 not even that fits in 54 % of the records;
  • one consultation and one vaccine need 1,112 B (median), so an NTAG216 holds a consultation in practically no record;
  • with three consultations and three vaccines, after DEFLATE, consultations are 61 % of the bytes, free clinical text 32 % and the identifiers of visits and vaccines 10 %.

The audit's main lever is the encoding (ADR 005, proposed in its own pull request: dictionary, typed values and a shorter record type). This ADR covers the other lever, which only product can pull: what the copy needs to carry for offline care. Every field it carries costs space on a device that is already short of it, and data minimization is a goal of its own for a record held on a device the guardian keeps.

docs.text:

An ambiguous match is appended as a new item. 29 B + 29 B 83 B + 83 B Prescriptions medicalHistory[].prescriptions Nowhere: captured in add_consultation_screen.dart, never displayed Keeps the stored visit; a top-level field the device leaves empty is not an edit (_edited_fields). Safe. 80 B 112 B Practitioner medicalHistory[].practitioner Consultations tab Same as prescriptions. Safe. 30 B 62 B Provider medicalHistory[].provider Consultations tab Same. Safe. 39 B 49 B Payer medicalHistory[].payer Consultations tab Same. Safe. 14 B 18 B Vaccinator and site vaccinationRecord[].administratedBy, administratedAt Site in the vaccines tab; vaccinator nowhere Keeps the stored vaccine. Safe. 29 B 60 B Consent details guardianInfo.consent, guardian2Info.consent Summary tab, edit-guardian sheet Restores the stored consent when the guardian is the same person, the copy carries none and the stored consent has a signature (_preserve_consent_signature). An unsigned stored consent is erased. 28 B 27 B Guardian documents documentType, documentNumber of each guardian Summary tab, edit-guardian sheet Erases them on the server: guardianInfo is taken from the incoming payload. "Safe" means the server cannot lose data: the stored item wins on a key match and an omitted top-level field is not counted as an edit. It does not mean the offline profile is unchanged: whatever the copy omits, the offline profile does not show.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Measured capacity of each option with the current encoding and the fitting rule that gives back entries that still fit (PR #182). Consultations and vaccines are averages over the 200 records; the most this history allows is 2.27 and 2.35.

Option Removes NTAG215: base does not fit NTAG215: vaccines NTAG216: records with ≥ 1 consultation NTAG216: consultations A. As today — 54 % 0.01 0 % 0.01 B. Identifiers item identifiers 54 % 0.08 2 % 0.02 C. History fields B + practitioner, provider, payer, vaccinator and site 54 % 0.35 8 % 0.08 D. Declarative consent details, guardian documents, address detail 4 % 0.24 2 % 0.02 E. C + D all of the above 4 % 1.31 22 % 0.22

Content alone does not make a consultation fit in an NTAG215, and it moves an NTAG216 from 0 % to at most 22 % of records with a consultation. Clinical text is what fills the device, and it can only be kept or dropped whole. The encoding of ADR 005 shrinks every row of the first table; the two decisions add up and the combination should be measured once both are taken.

docs.title: Proposal (for decision)
docs.text:
1. Prescriptions. No screen shows them today. Either the offline profile shows them (a UI change, then they stay) or the copy stops carrying them (safe for the sync, 80–112 B).
  2. Vaccinator. Not shown anywhere: stop carrying administratedBy (safe).
  3. Practitioner, provider, payer, vaccination site. Shown offline but administrative rather than clinical. Product decides whether offline care needs them; removing them is safe for the sync.
  4. Item identifiers. Keep for now. Removing them saves about 10 % but makes the sync depend on matching by start time or by date, vaccine and dose, and on the app's in-place edit of the last visit doing the same. Revisit only if the device is still short after ADR 005, with tests on both sides first.
  5. Consent details. The backend restores them only when the stored consent is signed. Before dropping them, either confirm that every stored consent has a signature or extend that rule to unsigned consents; then product decides whether the offline profile needs to show the consent.
  6. Guardian documents and address detail. Only after the backend preserves them when the copy omits them, as it already does for the consent signature.
  7. Clinical text and diagnoses. Keep, whole.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The on-chip format does not change: an omitted field is absent, and every build already reads an absent field as its default. Old and new builds can be mixed.
  • Every removal changes what the offline profile shows, for every patient, and the user guide has to say so.
  • A field removed today cannot be restored offline later: the copy only holds what it was written with. Choices that favor clinical content over administrative content are the reversible ones.
  • The numbers come from synthetic records. Before deciding on the identifiers or on the clinical text, measure the real distribution of sizes with the measurement tooling of the audit's recommendation 3.

docs.title: How the numbers were measured
docs.text: The NFC compression audit's harness (published in its own PR) generates 600 synthetic records with the app's builders, keeps 200 for measurement, removes each group from the guardian copy, encodes it exactly as the app does (alias, CBOR) and compresses it with the app's ZLibEncoder in Dart. Capacity uses the app's budgets (guardianPayloadBudget: 458 B and 838 B) and the AES-GCM overhead of 28 B. The fields each screen uses come from the presentation code (lib/src/features/nfc/presentation/); the sync behavior, from the backend's record_merger.py and app/schemas/patient.py.

docs.title: NFC Compression Audit
docs.text: Date: 2026-11-17 · Code audited: frontend develop at 25ec698; backend develop at d6fd83c for the sync behaviour · Benchmark: tool/nfc_compression_audit/ (full tables in its results.md)

docs.title: Question and short answer
docs.text:
Does the app use the best available algorithms and methods to compress what it writes to NFC chips?

The algorithm, yes; the method around it, no.

  • Algorithm. Without a dictionary, DEFLATE at level 9 is within 7 % of the best general-purpose compressor measured (zstd, brotli, LZMA2). Changing the compressor alone gains nothing.
  • Method. What is missing is what works for payloads of 100 to 2,000 bytes: a dictionary shared by writer and reader, an encoding without redundant fields or values stored as text, a short record type, and a fitting rule that does not leave out what fits.

With techniques the app already has, and no new dependency, today's NDEF messages are 1.6 to 3.2 times larger than they need to be:

Whole NDEF message, median Today Best practical, optimistic Best practical, pessimistic Triage (patient device) 178 B 77 B 90 B Guardian copy, no history 496 B 202 B 268 B Guardian copy, 1 consultation + 1 vaccine 1,112 B 352 B 645 B Guardian copy, 3 + 3 1,773 B 573 B 1,076 B

Best practical combines typed values without redundant keys, DEFLATE with a preset dictionary (8 KB for the triage, 32 KB for the guardian copy) and an external record type, with the same 28 B of AES-GCM. Pessimistic assumes the dictionary does nothing for free clinical text and names (see Limits).

Where it matters is the guardian copy. Today, on an NTAG215 (492 B), not even the copy without history fits in 54 % of the records, and on an NTAG216 (872 B) a consultation fits in practically none.

Payload format 2 as implemented (ADR 005, recommendation 2) keeps the key names, skips integer keys and default omission, which the dictionary makes cheap, and uses a 17-character external type instead of the 8 characters measured here. Measured with its own code, its medians are 89 B for the triage and 375 B for the guardian copy with 1 + 1, against 77 B and 352 B above.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Read:

  • the write and read paths of both chips: NfcTriagePayload, NfcGuardianPayload, nfc_guardian_alias.dart, NfcPayloadCodec, NfcPayloadService, the NDEF record, guardianPayloadBudget;
  • the screens that write chips (registration, profile actions) and those that show what is read;
  • the backend merge (record_merger.py, patient_service.py, schemas/patient.py), to know what a copy may leave out.

Out of scope:

  • key management and the design of the encryption (ADR 003, nfc-encryption.md);
  • the UI beyond which fields it shows.

docs.title: The pipeline as built
docs.text:
Paths and lines at 25ec698.

  1. Payload maps. Two builders produce them:
  2. NfcTriagePayload.buildPatientPayload writes the triage with hand-shortened keys (fn, dob, alg…).
  3. NfcGuardianPayload.buildGuardianPayload writes the whole PatientFullRecord.toJson(), minus the consent signature and the AI metadata of diagnoses, with at most the three most recent consultations and vaccines. aliasGuardianPayload then shortens 110 keys and adds a $v: 2 marker.
  4. Encoding (nfc_payload_codec.dart): CBOR (package cbor 6.5.1, which stores each float in its shortest lossless form), then raw DEFLATE level 9 (line 236, no dictionary), then AES-256-GCM. The encryption adds a 12-byte nonce and a 16-byte tag; from key version 1 on, also a 3-byte HW + version header, and the chip binding of ADR 003.
  5. Record (nfc_payload_service.dart:81, :92): one MIME record of type application/vnd.hwb.triage or application/vnd.hwb.guardian.
  6. Fit (nfc_guardian_payload.dart:117-129): the guardian copy is trimmed to the capacity the chip reports, alternating the oldest consultation and vaccine and stopping at the first combination that fits. The triage is never trimmed.
  7. Read (readHwbChip): find the MIME record, decrypt with the chip binding and then without it, inflate, decode the CBOR, rebuild the record.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
Corpus. 600 invented records: 400 for training dictionaries and models, 200 for measuring. corpus_test.dart generates them with the app's own builders.

  • Fields are filled as the registration, consultation and vaccine screens fill them.
  • Clinical text is Spanish, combined from phrase lists. Each list has entries that appear only in the test split, so dictionaries are not measured against their own training data.

Validation.

  • The benchmark reproduces the app's CBOR byte for byte for all 3,000 payloads (triage and guardian copies with 0 to 3 consultations and vaccines).
  • Every DEFLATE figure comes from the app's own dart:io zlib: Python's zlib 1.2.12 gives other sizes for the same bytes (−10 to +29 B on a 1 KB payload).
  • Every compressed payload with a dictionary was decompressed back and compared.

Encodings measured.

Triage Guardian copy Current T0 G0 (G0b: the alias table completed) Without redundant keys: a key is dropped only if what the app reconstructs stays identical, checked record by record T1 G1 + integer keys T2 G2 + typed values (UUIDs and chip UIDs as bytes, dates as day counts, date-times as minutes and offset, digit strings as integers) T3 G3 + catalog codes for closed or public lists T4 G4

Compressors.

  • none;
  • DEFLATE-9 as today;
  • DEFLATE-9 with an 8 KB or 32 KB dictionary made of training payloads;
  • zstd 1.5.7 at level 19, with or without a trained dictionary, without its 4-byte magic number;
  • brotli 1.2.0 at quality 11, with or without the same 32 KB dictionary;
  • raw LZMA2;
  • a context-model reference: bytes context of orders 0–3, Witten-Bell interpolation, trained on the training split, ideal arithmetic-coding length. A reference for what a trained statistical coder reaches, not a theoretical bound.

Capacity. The app's budgets, guardianPayloadBudget: 458 B on an NTAG215 and 838 B on an NTAG216 (capacity minus the MIME record overhead). Two algorithms: the app's own, and a full search over (consultations, vaccines) for what is achievable.

Current guardian copy with 3 + 3, after DEFLATE, share of the total that removing each part saves:

docs.title: Findings
docs.text:
H1. No preset dictionary. - Where: nfc_payload_codec.dart:236, ZLibEncoder(level: 9, raw: true). - Effect: at these sizes DEFLATE has no history of its own. The triage goes from 122 B to 120 B; with an 8 KB dictionary, to 55 B, without changing anything else. This is the largest lever.

H2. dart:io ignores a dictionary on raw streams. - What happens: ZLibEncoder(raw: true, dictionary: d) returns the same bytes as without it, and the decoder ignores it too, so a round-trip test passes while the dictionary does nothing. - What works: a raw stream primed by compressing the dictionary and flushing with Z_SYNC_FLUSH (the stream deflateSetDictionary produces, readable by any zlib, with no extra bytes), or the zlib format with the dictionary (4 B more). The benchmark checked both on 18,060 payloads.

H3. The fit leaves out what fits. - Where: nfc_guardian_payload.dart:117-129. - What happens: the trim alternates consultations and vaccines and stops at the first combination that fits. A consultation is several times larger than a vaccine, so vaccines are dropped in step with consultations. - Effect: on an NTAG216 the copy keeps 1.03 vaccines on average where 2.35 fit.

H4. Defaults are written. - What: keys whose absence leaves the reconstructed record identical are written to every chip. For example type: "Consultation", careModality: "01", diagnosisType: "01", status: "completed", intent: "order", country: "COL", policyVersion: "v1.1", and empty lists (riskFactors, prescriptions, allergies…). - Effect: 6 to 9 % after DEFLATE, almost nothing once there is a dictionary.

H5. Values stored as text. - What: UUIDs of visits and vaccines, dates, date-times and digit strings are written as text. - Effect: UUIDs are 10 % of a compressed guardian copy and dates 4 %. Typed values save 16 to 24 % even with a dictionary. - Alias table: it misses 9 keys the copy carries (prescriptions, frequency, duration, route, intent, weight, height, isBloodTypeCertified, baseVersion); completing it saves 2 to 5 %.

H6. A long record type. - Where: nfc_payload_service.dart:81 and :92. - Effect: the MIME types cost 29 to 34 B per chip; an 8-character external type costs 11 to 14 B. - Constraint: nothing in the OS depends on the type (no NFC intent filters, AndroidManifest.xml:36-45), but from key version 1 the type is part of the chip binding's associated data.

H7. btC is written and never read. - Where: the triage stores btC: true for a blood type confirmed by a test (nfc_triage_payload.dart:40), but fromPayload (:90) ignores it. - Effect: a record rebuilt from the patient device alone always shows the blood type as reported.

H8. Nothing measures real payloads. - What: the size of a write only shows when it does not fit (nfc_guided_write.dart:382). - Effect: nothing calibrates the decisions above, and the length of real clinical notes, which decides most of the remaining uncertainty, is unknown.

Already right. - Serialize, then compress, then encrypt: encrypted bytes do not compress. - CBOR is about 20 % smaller than JSON. - Raw DEFLATE carries no checksum of its own, which is correct because AES-GCM authenticates. - Level 9. - The 28 B of AES-GCM are the standard parameters and should stay.

docs.title: Recommendations and where they went
docs.text:
# Recommendation Pull request 1 Fit: give back what still fits after the trim (H3) guane-hwb/health-without-borders-frontend#182 2 Payload format 2: typed values, preset dictionary, external record (H1, H2, H5, H6); phase 1 reads both formats and writes format 1 guane-hwb/health-without-borders-frontend#185 (ADR 005) 3 Measure real payloads: write-size telemetry and a tool for existing records (H8) guane-hwb/health-without-borders-frontend#186 and guane-hwb/health-without-borders#106 4 Read btC (H7) guane-hwb/health-without-borders-frontend#183 5 Decide what the guardian copy carries offline guane-hwb/health-without-borders-frontend#184 (ADR 006)

Not recommended:

  • Moving to zstd or brotli: a native dependency for a single-digit gain over DEFLATE with a dictionary.
  • Shortening the AES-GCM nonce or tag: a security trade-off for 4 to 7 B.
  • Catalog codes for now: 4 to 6 % with a dictionary, at the cost of shipping and maintaining catalogs in the app.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The records are synthetic. Relative results hold, because the structure of the payloads is the app's own. Absolute sizes, and capacity above all, depend on how long real clinical notes are. The marginal costs above let them be scaled.
  • Dictionary gains on free text are bounded, not known. The synthetic text comes from closed phrase lists that the dictionary learns. The optimistic figure counts that; the pessimistic one gives the text no gain at all. Real notes fall in between. The tool of recommendation 3 measures them without any record leaving the authorised environment.
  • Chip capacities are those Android reports (492 and 872 B). Nothing was written to a physical chip.
  • The context model is a reference, not a bound. It is also trained on synthetic text.
  • The breakdown of where the bytes go uses Python's zlib. Read its shares, not its byte counts.

docs.title: Reproducing it
docs.text: See tool/nfc_compression_audit/README.md. Every step is deterministic, and results.md in that directory is the report this audit is based on.

docs.title: NFC encryption and the key ring
docs.text:
How the app encrypts what it writes to NFC chips, which key it uses, and why a reader sometimes refuses a chip it can physically see.

The operational side — generating keys, rotating, retiring, and the rules that silently destroy chip readability if broken — lives in the backend runbook: NFC Key Management. Read it before touching anything to do with keys in a deployed environment.

docs.title: What is on the chip
docs.text:
Every HWB chip — a patient device or a guardian card — carries its clinical payload in one of two formats, and every build since ADR 005 reads both:

format 1: JSON map → CBOR → DEFLATE → AES-256-GCM, in a MIME record
format 2: JSON map → typed CBOR → DEFLATE with a preset dictionary
          → AES-256-GCM, in an NFC Forum external record

lib/src/core/nfc/nfc_payload_codec.dart owns format 1 and the encryption of both; nfc_payload_v2.dart builds the format 2 plaintext. A build writes format 1 unless it was made with --dart-define=HWB_NFC_PAYLOAD_FORMAT=2 (kNfcWriteFormat; see ADR 005 before changing it). Both chip types go through the same NfcPayloadService and therefore the same key.

The chip's hardware UID is not encrypted and is always readable. That matters: a device with connectivity can resolve the patient from the UID alone through /patients/scan, even when it cannot decrypt the payload. The chip is a cache for offline use; the backend is the source of truth.

A guardian device holds the bounded record of one patient, so every minor needs a guardian device of their own. writeGuardianRecord(patientId: ...) refuses a chip that is a patient device or holds another patient's copy (NfcDeviceInUseException); registration checks the same when the guardian device is scanned. Offline, the reader uses the guardian copy only when its device_uid is the patient device just scanned; otherwise it shows the triage, read-only.

docs.title: How the guardian copy is fitted to the chip
docs.text:
The guardian copy carries at most the three most recent consultations and the three most recent vaccines. NfcGuardianPayload.buildWithinCapacity fits it to the capacity the chip reports, inside the tap, in two steps:

  1. Trim. While the encoded copy does not fit, drop the oldest entry of one history at a time, alternating between consultations and vaccines (a consultation first when both hold the same number).
  2. Give back. Once it fits, return to the history that was not cut last the entries it lost, one at a time, while they still fit.

The result leaves no entry out while there is room for it: adding the next consultation or the next vaccine would not fit. Without the second step the alternation dropped vaccines in step with consultations, and since a consultation is several times larger than a vaccine, a card with room for three vaccines was written with one. Each history keeps its most recent entries, so the partial-device notice ("the most recent entries were saved") stays accurate.

docs.title: Wire format
docs.text:
version 0 : [12-byte nonce][ciphertext][16-byte auth tag]
version 1+: ['H']['W'][version][nonce][ciphertext][tag]

For version 1 and above, the three header bytes are passed to AES-GCM as associated data, so the version byte cannot be stripped or edited without failing authentication.

Version 0 deliberately writes no header. This is not an oversight. A build that predates key versioning reads the first bytes as the nonce, so a header there would make everything written by a newer build unreadable to an older one — during any partial rollout, which is the normal state of a device fleet. A header only ever appears once a deployment rotates to version 1.

decode() reads both layouts. For a headerless payload it reports the version whose key succeeded, which is the version the chip is effectively on.

The envelope is the same in both payload formats. What it encloses differs:

Payload format Record Plaintext inside the envelope 1 MIME application/vnd.hwb.triage / …guardian DEFLATE of CBOR 2 external guane.com.co:hwbt / …:hwbg [2][dictionary id] + DEFLATE, primed with that dictionary, of typed CBOR

The chip binding of ADR 003 puts the record type in the associated data, so a payload cannot be moved between formats either.

docs.title: The key ring, not a key
docs.text:
The backend delivers a ring — version -> key — at login, refresh and /users/me. NfcKeyring (lib/src/core/nfc/nfc_keyring.dart) holds it; AuthRepository.getNfcKeyring() is the single accessor.

A device that holds a ring sends X-NFC-Keyring-Fingerprint on refresh and /users/me: a SHA-256 over the keys and the current version it holds. If it matches, the backend does not send the ring again, and the response without keys leaves the held ring in place. Any change to the ring changes the fingerprint, so the next refresh delivers it. Login and the password change always deliver it. The web build holds no ring: the backend does not deliver keys to a browser.

Reads resolve whichever version the chip names. Writes use the ring's current version.

Always build the codec from the ring

NfcPayloadCodec(hexKey: ...) stamps version 0 into the header while encrypting with whatever key it was handed. After a rotation that produces a chip no reader can decrypt — silently and permanently. This is not hypothetical: it is a defect that reached develop once and had to be fixed. Use NfcPayloadCodec.fromKeyring(keyring: ...).

A malformed key in the ring is dropped with a log line rather than rejected wholesale, so one bad key delivered by the backend degrades that version instead of disabling NFC entirely. If the dropped version happens to be the current one, the codec becomes read-only: it refuses to write rather than encrypt with a guessed key.

docs.title: The session window
docs.text:
The ring is only served while the refresh token's exp is still in the future. The claim is read locally from the JWT, so the check works with no connectivity — which is the point.

Outside the window the ring is wiped from memory and from disk, and NFC reads and writes are refused. The session itself is still restored, because the device may hold unsynced records the health worker needs to see; what appears is the persistent SessionWindowBanner telling them to reconnect.

The window slides forward on every successful refresh, so someone using the app normally never meets it. Reaching it requires roughly a week with no connectivity at all.

docs.title: Clock handling
docs.text:
The window is judged against the device clock, so a stored high-water mark (hwb_clock_mark) detects the clock being moved backwards: more than 24 hours behind the mark closes the window. The tolerance absorbs NTP corrections and timezone changes.

The mark is re-anchored to the server's clock — the refresh token's iat — on every successful login and refresh. Without that, a device whose clock ran ahead even briefly would keep a mark in the future and refuse NFC until real time caught up, with no way out but clearing app storage, which destroys pending records.

docs.title: Key version telemetry
docs.text:
Every chip read records which key version opened it, keyed by device UID in nfc_key_version_observations, with a patient / guardian role. SyncEngine ships pending observations and marks them reported only after the server confirms.

This exists for one operational question: can a key version be retired without leaving chips unreadable offline? A version 0 chip carries no hint of its version at all (from version 1 on, the version byte is in the clear header), and either way only a device that reads the chip learns it, so measuring is the only way to know how far a rotation has drained.

The UID stays on the phone. The backend stores an HMAC of it, not the UID, keeps each sighting for 730 days, and drops sightings of versions that do not exist (backend docs/infrastructure/nfc-key-management.md, "Telemetry storage").

observed_at is stored and sent in UTC. A naive local timestamp is read by the server as UTC and shifts every sighting by the device's offset.

The whole path is best-effort: every failure is caught and logged. A lost observation delays a rotation decision; a broken read leaves a clinician with no history in front of a patient. Those are not comparable, and the code treats them accordingly.

docs.title: Write-size telemetry
docs.text:
Every successful chip write records its sizes in nfc_write_metrics, and SyncEngine reports them to POST /api/v1/patients/nfc-write-metrics. The question they answer is how the payload format and the guardian copy should change: how close each write comes to the chip's capacity, and how often the guardian copy had to leave history out.

Field Patient device Guardian device device_role patient guardian payload_format, key_version format of the payload (1 today) and key version same payload_bytes, message_bytes, chip_capacity encrypted payload, whole NDEF message, capacity the chip reported same consultations_kept/total, vaccines_kept/total null what the copy kept, of what it would carry on a chip with room for everything (the most recent, at most 3): kept < total means the chip's capacity left history out written_at UTC UTC

No UID, no patient, no record content: a row cannot be traced back to a person. NfcPayloadService builds the metric after write() returns and hands it to the onWritten observer without awaiting it; a failure is logged and the write is unaffected. The table keeps at most LocalDatabase.maxPendingNfcWriteMetrics rows (the newest), and rows are deleted as soon as the server accepts them. The web build writes no chips and stores nothing.

The same sizes for records that already exist, before any build reports them, come from tool/nfc_measure/ (aggregates only; read its README before running it on real records).

docs.title: Updating the fleet
docs.text:
The build compatibility rule that matters, in both directions:

Chip written by Read by older build Read by current build Older build (no versioning) ✅ ✅ Current build, version 0 ✅ ✅ Current build, version 1+ ❌ ✅

So while the current version is 0, builds are interchangeable in both directions and a partial rollout is safe.

The payload format follows the same rule. A build before ADR 005 does not know format 2 and sees such a chip as blank, so format 2 is written only after every device runs a build that reads it (phase 2 of ADR 005):

Chip written in Read by a build before ADR 005 Read by a build with it Format 1 ✅ ✅ Format 2 ❌ (blank) ✅

Before any rotation

The current version must stay at 0 until every device runs a build that understands the ring. An older build takes the current key, ignores the ring, and loses the ability to read everything written under version 0. Confirm the fleet first; the backend runbook has the procedure.

Where the current version is set depends on the backend's mode. The pilot keeps the ring in its database under a KEK: there the current version only changes through POST /api/v1/patients/nfc-keys/rotate (or /revoke of the current version) and automatic rotation (NFC_AUTO_ROTATE), and NFC_CURRENT_KEY_VERSION is ignored. That variable only applies to a deployment without a KEK, which serves the ring from its environment.

As of the current build, no rotation has occurred: every chip in the field is version 0, headerless.

docs.title: Offline Guardian Factor & Threat Model Considerations
docs.text:
When operating without connectivity, the requirement for a guardian card before opening a minor's profile is enforced locally by the application interface (read_nfc_screen.dart):

  1. Local Decryption: The patient wristband payload (triage) is encrypted with the fleet-wide keyring. Once scanned, the client decrypts the payload in memory to inspect demographic fields (dob, isMinor) and identity linkages (gUid, g2Uid).
  2. Access Control Enforcement: If the patient is determined to be a minor (isMinor == true), the UI transitions to the second factor step demanding a scan of the guardian card matching gUid or g2Uid. If absent, only the read-only emergency triage flow (logged via logEmergencyAccess) is permitted.
  3. Accepted Risk: In an offline architecture utilizing a shared symmetric keyring, cryptographic enforcement of guardian presence cannot be guaranteed against a maliciously modified client application, because the client already holds the decrypted triage data in memory. This risk is accepted by design:
  4. Encrypting the guardian payload separately under a secret key held exclusively on the physical guardian card would prevent multi-brigade read-only triage in emergency situations.
  5. Genuine offline operations prioritize life-saving clinical triage (break-glass) while recording audit events locally for deferred backend synchronization.

docs.title: NFC Payload Size: Options Beyond Format 2
docs.text: Date: 17 November 2026. Builds on: ADR 005 (format 2), the NFC compression audit and ADR 006 (what the guardian copy carries). Measurements: tool/nfc_size_options/, whose report is tool/nfc_size_options/results.md.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Format 2 brings the guardian copy (3 consultations and 3 vaccines) to a median NDEF message of 1,852.5 B with normal clinical text and 2,550 B with long text. What is left is mostly free clinical text: 29 % of the copy with normal text and 49 % with long text, stored at 3.0 and 2.3 bits per character.

  • Content decisions can still move the chip; encoding no longer can. Keeping free clinical text only in the most recent consultation, together with ADR 006 option C, takes the copy down 31.9 % (normal text) and 38.4 % (long text). Every full copy in the corpus then fits a DESFire EV3 2K, long text included: the largest is 1,880 B of ~1,900 B. Neither needs a format change.
  • Encoding levers are small. Digit-only phones save 0.5 %, an NDEF record without type and a merged header 1.1 %, and text rebuilt from catalogs the app already ships 1.6 %. An ICD-10/ICD-11 catalog in the app would save 5.9 %, but the app does not ship one.
  • Tokenization pays only with entropy coding. A subword vocabulary with fixed probabilities and an arithmetic coder could take the copy down an estimated 8 to 14 % with normal text; this is not measured. Bare token ids, an LLM tokenizer and neural compression do not fit the app.
  • The patient device stays on NTAG215. Even with every lever, the triage fits an NTAG213 for 50 of 100 patients.

All figures come from the app's own code on a synthetic corpus calibrated against the NFC capacity analysis of 21 October 2026; see Limits.

docs.title: Where format 2 leaves the bytes
docs.text:
Measure Normal text Long text Full copy, median NDEF message (B) 1,852.5 2,550 Full copies within a DESFire EV3 2K, ~1,900 B (of 100) 63 0 Free clinical text, share of the copy (%) 29.4 48.7 Free clinical text per copy, median (characters) 1,440.5 4,258.5 Cost of that text in format 2 (bits per character) 3.00 2.34 The same, per word (bits) 17.1 13.4

The rest of the copy is the fixed part (patient, guardians, background, allergies), identifiers and dates (already typed by format 2), codes, and 54 B of wrapping: 31 B of AES-GCM seal with the key header and 23 B of NDEF record.

docs.title: Levers measured
docs.text:
Each lever is applied on top of format 2 as built and measured with format 2's own encoder and dictionary 1 (NDEF message, median of 100 patients). The full table, with the long-text maxima, is in tool/nfc_size_options/results.md.

Lever Kind Normal text (%) Long text (%) Full copies within 2K, normal · long (of 100) Format 2 as built — 1,852.5 B 2,550 B 63 · 0 Free clinical text only in the most recent consultation Content −17.5 −28.3 100 · 70 ADR 006, option C Content −12.5 −9.6 100 · 0 Each clinical text field cut to 160 characters Content (drops text) −2.2 −26.1 75 · 55 Text rebuilt from an ICD-10/ICD-11 catalog Encoding, new catalog −5.9 −3.8 90 · 0 Text rebuilt from catalogs the app ships (vaccine, country) Encoding −1.6 −1.5 71 · 0 Text rebuilt from a DANE catalog (city, department) Encoding, new catalog −0.7 −0.4 67 · 0 Phones stored as digits only App input −0.5 −0.1 67 · 0 NDEF record without type, merged header Encoding −1.1 −0.8 — ADR 006 (C) and text only in the latest consultation Content −31.9 −38.4 100 · 100 The same, with digit phones and the catalogs the app ships Content, encoding −34.0 −39.9 100 · 100 The same, with ICD and DANE catalogs too Content, encoding, new catalogs −39.6 −44.6 100 · 100 No free clinical text at all (ceiling of any text lever) — −29.4 −48.7 100 · 100

The audit measured three more levers on its own corpus, which are not repeated here. Integer keys and catalog codes stored as integers save 3 to 4 % each with a dictionary, and up to 14 % without one. zstd with a dictionary saves 6 to 8 % against DEFLATE with a dictionary, at the cost of a native library on Android, iOS and web.

docs.title: What each lever needs
docs.text:
• Free text only in the latest consultation (content). Older consultations keep every other field: dates, diagnoses and prescriptions. Offline, the profile would show them without notes. It changes what NfcGuardianPayload.buildGuardianPayload puts in, not the format: PatientFullRecord.fromJson gives every field a default, so readers already accept a consultation without clinicalEvaluation. On sync, the server keeps its own version of a consultation it already holds (merged by encounterIdentifier), so a copy without older notes should not erase them. As with ADR 006, a backend test must confirm it before this ships.
  • ADR 006, option C (content). The decision is open in #184.
  • Text rebuilt from catalogs (encoding). Readers must rebuild what writers leave out, so this is a format change: a new format byte or dictionary id, with the two-phase rollout of ADR 005. It is lossless only if the copy keeps the text whenever it differs from the catalog's, and if the catalog version travels with the payload.
    • The app ships the vaccine catalog (add_vaccine_screen.dart) and the country catalog (country_display.dart).
    • The app does not ship an ICD catalog. The backend loads the WHO ICD-10 (~12,600 entries, displays mostly in English) and ICD-11 MMS (~34,700 entries) catalogs; the app would need at least the codes in use.
    • A DANE catalog of municipalities is small, but it gains only 0.7 %.
  • Digit-only phones (app input). The registration form stores the number as typed (its hint is +57 310 482 9914). Normalizing it when saving lets format 2 store it as an integer; formatting it for display becomes the app's job.
  • NDEF record without type (encoding). It saves 17 B per chip, plus 3 B from merging the key header with the format and dictionary bytes. The type is what lets the platform route a tag to the app and tells an HWB chip from other NDEF content, so it is worth it only where 20 B matter: the triage.
  • Text cap (content). It drops text. On long text it gains as much as dropping older notes, but the reader cannot tell what was cut.

docs.title: Tokenization
docs.text:
A tokenizer helps only if each token is coded by its probability, not by its id. Format 2 already works like one: each string its dictionary matches costs 2 to 3 B, which pays for long phrases and not for short words.

Option How it works What it would save What it costs 1. Catalog codes ("tokens with meaning") Store the ICD, ATC/CUM, vaccine or DANE code instead of its text; the app rebuilds the text Measured above: up to 8.3 % of the copy Versioned catalogs in the app; works only for text that came from a catalog 2. Fixed vocabulary with ids Each frequent word becomes a 1- or 2-byte id; the rest is spelled out Little or nothing: 8 to 16 bits per word against 17 today, and the long phrases the dictionary already covers are lost Simple, but does not pay 3. Subwords with fixed probabilities A vocabulary of 4,000 to 8,000 pieces (BPE or Unigram, as in SentencePiece) trained on public Spanish clinical text; an arithmetic coder stores each piece in −log₂ p bits, with a fallback to single characters Estimated, not measured: 8 to 14 % of the copy with normal text, if the text drops from 3.0 to 1.6–2.2 bits per character A codec of our own in Dart with integer arithmetic; a 50 to 150 KB model versioned like the dictionary; a new format 4. An LLM's tokenizer A vocabulary of 32,000 to 200,000 tokens; each id takes 15 to 18 bits Worse than today without a model to give probabilities: about 4 to 5 bits per character Vocabulary files of several MB, and their licences 5. Compression with a language model A network predicts each token and the arithmetic coder stores only the surprise The best ratio, about 1 bit per character A model of tens to hundreds of MB, slow on a phone; decoding needs bit-identical results on Android, iOS and web, which floating point does not guarantee

Any of them must keep the conditions format 2 keeps:

  • No patient data in the vocabulary or the model. They ship inside a public app, so they come from public sources (ICD descriptions, the medication catalog, public clinical guidelines) or synthetic text.
  • Versioned for good. A payload says which model wrote it, and a model written in the field is readable forever.
  • Deterministic, and checked before writing. The same input gives the same bits on every device, and the payload is decoded back before it is written.
  • Bounded by the text. Even free text would leave the copy at most 29 % (normal) or 49 % (long) smaller.

docs.title: Patient device
docs.text:
Lever on the triage (format 2) Median (B) Maximum (B) Within an NTAG213, 137 B (of 100) Format 2 as built 183.5 297 19 Guardian phone as digits 178.5 289 21 And chronic conditions as ICD-10 codes 157 234 37 And an NDEF record without type, with the merged header 137 214 50

The NTAG215 stays for the patient device. What still weighs most in the triage is the allergies, whose reactions are free text.

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text:
1. Decide the content levers first. ADR 006 option C and keeping notes only for the latest consultation need no format change, and together they let a DESFire EV3 2K hold every full copy of this corpus. They are product decisions; the second one would extend ADR 006.
  2. Measure real sizes before buying chips or building a codec. #186 and the backend's #106 report the size of every write, with no clinical content.
  3. If more is needed afterwards, ship an ICD catalog subset with a format change (5.9 %), keeping the text whenever it differs from the catalog's.
  4. Prototype the subword coder offline only if real notes turn out to be text-heavy, and compare it with DEFLATE and dictionary 1 on the same text.
  5. Not recommended: an LLM's tokenizer or neural compression; shortening the AES-GCM tag or nonce (4 to 12 B for weaker authentication); dropping the record type of the guardian copy.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
• Code. The branch of #185 (a30f711): format 2's encoder, dictionary 1 and record builder; format 1's codec and fit, which are develop's.
  • Corpus. gen_corpus.py rebuilds the corpus the 21 October analysis described (that corpus is not versioned): 100 patients, 49 with two guardians, 0 to 3 allergies in its proportions, every field of the model filled in, and histories of 10 consultations taken from other patients with 1 or 2 diagnoses. The long-text variant joins each clinical field with those of two other consultations. Its vocabulary was written apart from the audit's generator, which is what dictionary 1 was built from.
  • Calibration. On format 1 as written today the corpus lands close to the 21 October figures: median triage 253 B against 263 B, and a compressed full copy 10 % larger. Section 1 of results.md sets every figure side by side.
  • Levers. levers_test.dart applies each lever to the aliased copy or the triage and measures it with NfcPayloadV2.plaintextSize; report.py adds the seal and the record, both measured with the app's code.
  • Reproducing it. tool/nfc_size_options/README.md has the commands. Every step is deterministic; a fresh run gives the same results.md.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The data is synthetic. How well dictionary 1 and any tokenizer do on real clinical notes is not known.
  • The tokenization figures are an estimate from an assumed 1.6 to 2.2 bits per character, not a measurement.
  • The DESFire capacities are those of the 21 October analysis: ~1,900 B for the 2K comes from a vendor; the 4K and 8K figures are assumptions.
  • The sync safety of dropping older notes rests on the merge rule for stored consultations and still needs a backend test.
  • The corpus stores nationality codes as numbers where the app uses ISO alpha-3 codes; the difference is at most 1 B per record.

docs.title: Offline-first and synchronization
docs.text: The app is designed to work without an internet connection. This page explains how data is stored locally and how it is synchronized with the backend when a network connection is available.

docs.title: Local storage — LocalDatabase
docs.text:
lib/src/core/storage/local_database.dart is a singleton that wraps sqflite (on mobile and desktop) and IndexedDB (on Web).

Schema of the local_patients table:

CREATE TABLE local_patients (
  patient_id    TEXT PRIMARY KEY, -- UUID v4 generated by the frontend
  device_uid    TEXT NOT NULL, -- NFC device UID
  patient_name  TEXT NOT NULL, -- Name to display in the UI (masked)
  record_json   TEXT NOT NULL, -- PatientFullRecord serialized as JSON (encrypted)
  is_synced     INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, -- 0 = pending, 1 = synchronized
  sync_error    TEXT, -- Message of the last sync error
  sync_error_code INTEGER, -- HTTP status code of the last sync error
  created_at    TEXT NOT NULL, -- ISO 8601
  synced_at     TEXT, -- ISO 8601 — null until the first successful sync
  revision      INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  owner_user_id TEXT,
  organization_id TEXT,
  pending_retired_reason TEXT
)

Almacenamiento en Web

sqflite is not available in Flutter Web. LocalDatabase uses IndexedDB (backed by hwb_local_store) as its persistence layer on Web, not just a development fallback — it is the production storage path for this platform. Encryption keys on Web are kept in sessionStorage (so ciphertexts in IndexedDB become unreadable upon closing the tab/session). Clinical payloads (record_json) are encrypted with AES-256-GCM before being written, the index patient_name column is masked (e.g. "Ana G.") rather than stored in full, and the break-glass emergency log encrypts patient_name/user_id the same way. See web/index.html's Content-Security-Policy for the defense-in-depth layer.

docs.title: Synchronization Engine — SyncEngine
docs.text: lib/src/core/sync/sync_engine.dart implements the background synchronization cycle.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
// Start connectivity monitoring
syncEngine.start();

// Stop (example, on logout)
syncEngine.stop();

docs.title: Synchronization Flow
docs.text:
Connectivity Detected (via connectivity_plus)
        │
        ▼
getUnsyncedRecords()   ← list local_patients WHERE is_synced = 0 AND owner_user_id = current_user
        │
        ▼ (for each record)
POST /api/v1/patients/sync
        │
   ┌────┴────┐
   │  201    │  → markSynced(patientId)   → removes the row from local storage
   │  4xx    │  → markSyncError(message)  → permanent error (holds/blocks row for review)
   │  5xx    │  → markSyncError(message)  → automatic retry
   │  401    │  → stop sync               → redirect to login
   └─────────┘

docs.title: Behavior by Error Code
docs.text:
Code Action 201 Marks as synchronized and deletes the row from local storage (markSynced)Marks as synchronized and deletes the row from local storage (markSynced) 400 / 403 / 409 / 422 Permanent error — holds row as blocked for review or user resolution 401 Stops synchronization entirely — token expired, requires re-login 408 / 429 / 502 / 503 / 504 Transient: keeps is_synced = 0 and is retried for good; never blocked, whatever its code 500, unexpected errors Keeps is_synced = 0 for automatic retry; after 8 attempts (maxSyncAttemptsBeforeBlocked) the row is blocked as 422 for review 503 sync_in_progress Another request was creating the same new patient (a retry racing the first attempt). Kept pending, not blocked, and retried no sooner than Retry-After (5 s) or the backoff, whichever is longer; the retry merges into the record the other request created. The queue shows it as pending Timeout, no connection Keeps is_synced = 0 and is retried for good, online or offline; never blocked

Transient failures (408, 429, 5xx, network) schedule the next attempt whether they come from a background cycle or from Sync now on one record. Only a failure of the record's own (a 500, an unexpected error) can block it once it has had 8 attempts; not reaching the server and the transient statuses never block it, so a device that stays offline, or a backend that is down for hours, does not block the queue.

docs.title: Record versions and conflicts
docs.text:
/scan and /search return the server's recordVersion. The app keeps it on PatientFullRecord.recordVersion and sends it back to /sync as baseVersion: the version its copy was based on. toJson() writes it under that name, and fromJson() reads it back from it, so the version survives the local queue and the guardian device.

A /sync that the server accepts (201) answers with record_version (the version after this sync) and conflicts (the parts it kept as it had them, for example stale_payload_base_version when baseVersion was older than its own). Two more codes have their own message in SyncConflictCode.describe: missing_base_version (a copy without baseVersion, from an older build or a guardian device written before the record had a version, would have removed allergies or background items, and the server kept them) and identity_edit_not_applied (names, birth date, sex or document differ from the server's, which a sync never changes). Any other code gets a generic line. The engine announces every saved record on SyncEngine.savedRecords:

  • The open profile adopts the new version, so its next edit is not taken for an old copy. An edit made while the sync was in flight is saved again on top of the new version.
  • When conflicts is not empty, the engine marks both chips for rewriting and stores a notice (sync_notices table, one per patient, masked name) that the sync queue lists until the user dismisses it. If the server sends its merged record back (record), the profile shows it; otherwise the copy keeps its old version, so anything edited next is merged rather than applied over the server's.
  • If only the FHIR delivery failed, the row stays queued to re-send the bundles and is moved onto the new version, since it holds exactly what was saved.

docs.title: Records of another user
docs.text: Every row carries owner_user_id. The engine, the sync queue and the home counts select the signed-in user's rows (and ownerless rows, which the first sync adopts). Another user's pending rows stay on the device, encrypted and unlisted, until that user signs in again; the queue shows how many there are via _foreignPendingCount to alert the active worker. Signing in as someone else does not overwrite or discard them.

docs.title: Operational Policy & Resolution Path (Pilot Protocol)
docs.text:
In clinical field missions with staff turnover, pending records left behind by a previous professional are handled as follows: 1. Field Handover Protocol: Before rotating tablets or swapping brigade shifts, staff must perform a manual sync (Sync all) while connectivity is available. 2. Re-authentication on Same Device: If records remain pending, the original author must log in on the device to complete the sync. 3. Supervisor / Admin Recovery Escalation: If the author has permanently left the mission, the physical device must be presented to an authorized Organization Administrator (org_admin). Under the supervised procedure, the admin coordinates session elevation or backend account re-authentication to drain the local queue, preventing data loss before decommissioning or reassigning the tablet.

AuthRepository.clearSession() deletes only the session's keys on a phone. On the web it still deletes everything, and logout wipes the local PHI.

The local database's AES keys are not in the session's store:

  • Android: LocalDatabase uses its own storageNamespace (hwb_local_db), with its own data file, KeyStore alias and wrapped key. A deleteAll() on the session store, or the plugin wiping that store after an error, does not reach them. A device updated from an older build still has them in the session store; the first time the database opens it copies them over, checks the copy and deletes the old one. That is why clearSession() still deletes key by key. The namespace needs flutter_secure_storage 10.1 or later: 10.0 opened one file per process, so a second store name was silently ignored.
  • iOS/macOS: a device-only keychain item under its own account.
  • A failed read never generates a new key. The database store sets resetOnError: false. With the plugin default, a failed read deletes the key and answers "nothing stored", so a new key would be generated and every local record would become unreadable. The read now ends in LocalKeyUnavailableException, and the records stay on the device for a later attempt.

docs.title: Retired devices
docs.text:
A lost, damaged or replaced patient or guardian device still holds its data, and offline the reader opens a record from the devices alone. Online the server answers 410 device_retired; offline the reader checks a local list first.

  • The list. GET /api/v1/patients/retired-devices returns, for every retired device, sha256("hwb-retired-device:v1:" + UID) with the UID reduced to its hex digits in upper case (retiredDeviceHash in lib/src/core/nfc/retired_device_hash.dart). The phone keeps hashes, not UIDs. The test vectors are shared with the backend (tests/contract/fixtures/retired_device_hashes.json there).
  • Download. Each syncAll() cycle, once the backend is reachable, asks for what was retired since the last server_time and stores it with the new one (tables retired_devices and retired_devices_cursor, schema v12). A failure keeps the previous list. clearAll() keeps it: it belongs to no user.
  • Learned on the spot. A 410 device_retired from /scan, and the old UIDs of a reassignment made on this phone, go into the list right away.
  • Offline read. A retired patient device is refused with the same message as online, without the guardian step or emergency access. A retired guardian device is refused, and the guardian step stays open for the new one.
  • Never downloaded. Until the first list arrives, a record still opens offline, with a warning that the device could not be checked.
  • Storage errors answer "not retired": a local failure never blocks care.

docs.title: Scrubbing of Clinical Data
docs.text:
Once a record is successfully synchronized with the backend (HTTP 201), the app removes the entry from local storage (markSynced deletes the row in local_patients).

This protects patient privacy in case of device loss or theft.
